content: The increased severity of the Chikungunya outbreak, which began in 2005, is believed to be linked to a mutation in the virus's genetic sequence. This mutation altered the virus's coat protein, potentially enhancing its ability to replicate in mosquito cells and enabling it to use the Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus) as a vector, in addition to the primary vector, Aedes aegypti. In July 2006, researchers analyzed the virus's RNA and identified specific genetic changes responsible for the heightened virulence of recent strains. The outbreak was first recorded in February 2005 on Réunion Island in the Indian Ocean. By May 18, 2006, approximately 258,000 residents (out of a population of 777,000) had been affected, with 219 deaths officially attributed to the virus. Neighboring regions, including Mauritius, Madagascar, the Comoros, Mayotte, and the Seychelles, also reported cases. In India, particularly in Nandurbar city, Maharashtra, many elderly individuals succumbed to complications associated with Chikungunya. Even three months post-infection, patients continued to experience severe morning joint pain, dyspepsia, relapsing fever, and joint swelling. Physicians were advised to monitor for platelet count abnormalities indicative of Dengue or Falciparum Malaria. In 2006, a significant outbreak occurred in Andhra Pradesh, India, with initial cases reported in Hyderabad, Secunderabad, and Anantpur district as early as November and December 2005. The outbreak persisted, with practitioners in Hyderabad alone seeing 10 to 20 cases daily. Some deaths were reported, primarily attributed to the misuse of antibiotics and anti-inflammatory medications. Severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and glycemic control issues were the primary causes of morbidity. Recovery was typical, though 3-5% of cases resulted in prolonged arthritis. The virus's ability to cause thrombocytopenia made the inappropriate use of certain drugs, such as steroids for joint pain, particularly dangerous, as it could lead to gastric erosions and life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding. By mid-2006, Southern India experienced a large-scale outbreak, with over 80,000 cases reported in Karnataka's districts, including Gulbarga, Tumkur, Bidar, Raichur, Bellary, and others. In March 2006, Malegaon town in Maharashtra reported over 2,000 cases, while Orissa state documented up to 5,000 cases of fever with muscle aches and headaches between February 27 and March 5, 2006. Bangalore, Karnataka's capital, also faced an outbreak in May 2006, with symptoms such as arthritis, arthralgia, and rashes. Tamil Nadu reported 20,000 cases in June 2006, with the disease spreading from Bangalore's outskirts into the city. By July 2006, over 300,000 people in Karnataka were affected, and Tamil Nadu saw nearly 100,000 cases by August 2006, with Chennai being one of the worst-hit areas. The Andaman Islands reported their first Chikungunya cases in June 2006, escalating to thousands by September, with relapsed cases presenting severe lower limb pain, vomiting, and general weakness. By August 24, 2006, 1.1 million cases were reported across Indian states, including Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, and Kerala. Despite government claims of no deaths, the epidemic's severity was evident, with significant outbreaks in Salem, Erode, and Coimbatore. In September 2006, western India, particularly Gujarat, experienced outbreaks following heavy rainfall and flooding. Goa also reported cases, with 5,000 individuals affected. Rajasthan saw thousands of cases in districts like Rajasamand, Bhilwara, and Udaipur after August floods, though media and government coverage was limited. By late September, cases were reported in Delhi and even among travelers returning to the United Kingdom. Symptoms included rash, fever, muscle and joint pain, and severe headache, with fatigue persisting for weeks post-illness. By October 2006, Kerala reported 61 deaths and 30,000 hospital admissions due to Chikungunya, with private clinic numbers unknown. The disease spread to Uttar Pradesh, with confirmed cases in Etawah and Kanpur by mid-October. By September 2007, the outbreak had reached Europe, with 130 confirmed cases in Ravenna, Italy, and one death reported.
